newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia oppn calls for native title plan changes.
newsitem.headline: Australia oppn calls for native title plan changes.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard faced some substantial changes to his native title plan if it was to pass through the upper house of parliament, the Senate, the opposition said on Monday.

Opposition justice spokesman Nick Bolkus said Howard's 10-point plan currently had major discriminatory and constitutional problems and these would have to be addressed if the government wanted to win Labor's support in the Senate.
Howard is expected to meet opposition leader Kim Beazley on the issue some time this week, although no specific date has yet been set.

"I think John Howard deep down knows that his plan, as it now stands, has got problems in terms of discrimination and problems in terms of the constitution," Bolkus told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"He's going to have to consider some fairly substantial changes to it whether, at this stage, or not he likes it.
"The plan has got some pretty fundamental constitutional problems which I think the meeting this week, if it takes place with Kim Beazley, will be quite useful."
The meeting between the two leaders is aimed at lessening the chances of an early election over racial issues.

Under the Australian consitution, the government can dissolve both houses of parliament and call an early election -- known as a double dissolution election -- if the non-government dominated senate twice rejects government legislation.

The government can then hold a joint sitting of both houses, using its large majority in the House of Representatives to push through contentious legislation, such as the plan to end the bitter land rights row between farmers and Aborigines.
Deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans said the Labor opposition was hopeful of finding some common ground with the government over native title, saying the alternative was not an attractive one.

"We're facing a knock-down, drag-out brawl on the issue in the Senate, culminating possibly in a double dissolution. (It) would be absolutely disastrous for any election to be fought on race-related issues in this country," Evans told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"It's in everybody's interest to take a deep breath and look again at a way through this tangle which will deliver not only a decent result for indigenous people, but a sensible result for pastoralists, miners and the taxpaying Australian community."
Howard's plan guarantees farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, while also allowing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.

Native title laws were introduced by the former Labor government three years ago, but became an urgent political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers could be liable to Aboriginal claim.
Howard is expected to publish draft legislation later this month.
